meeting_header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (Sentinel Head of ML), Elena Gomez (Sentinel SRE), Tom Li (Sentinel CTO), Nina Park (Sentinel PM)
summary: Discovery focused on latency and throughput requirements for Sentinel Payments. They are evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; primary concerns are p95 latency < 300ms for short streaming responses, concurrency ~150-200 concurrent users for chat-like flows, and batch token/sec throughput for nightly reconciliation jobs. Action: Redwood to run tailored latency benchmarks and share security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Monroe: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. Quick intros?
[00:08] Mark Rivera: Hi Mark here, head of ML at Sentinel. Elena SRE, Tom CTO, Nina PM.
[00:12] Priya Kapoor: Priya SE, I'll handle the performance bits.
[00:18] Alex Monroe: Great. We put a short agenda — latency/throughput, streaming, dedicated vs hosted, then next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Tom Li: Yep, let's jump in.
[01:02] Mark Rivera: To frame this — we're building a payments assistant that runs in-app chat and also does batch reconciliation. For chat, target is p95 under 300 milliseconds for short prompts (under 64 tokens) with streaming enabled. Concurrently we expect around 150 to 200 active users at peak. For batch jobs we care about tokens/sec for throughput to finish nightly runs.
[01:25] Priya Kapoor: Got it. Couple clarifying Qs — when you say streaming for chat, are you doing partial tokens to users as we generate? And are you attaching any tool calls or external DB fetches in the loop?
[01:34] Mark Rivera: Yes streaming, token-by-token to the app. We do a thin service call for user context before the model, but we try to keep per-request preproc under 20ms. No heavy tool loops on the critical path.
[01:47] Priya Kapoor: That helps. For p95 under 300ms that usually implies keeping end-to-end token generation in the 150-200ms range on the inference side for small sequences, depending on model size and batching. With streaming enabled, you'd see some latency savings on first byte but the tail can vary.
[02:05] Elena Gomez: When you say "model size" — what are we comparing? We're evaluating a 7B distilled model and a 13B quantized variant. Which one do we expect to hit those numbers with?
[02:16] Samir Patel: Short answer: 7B is much easier to meet the sub-300ms p95 for short sequences, especially with quantization and prefix caching. 13B can too, but typically needs dedicated GPU pools (A10/A100-style) and careful batching tuning. Also sequence length and kv-cache hits matter a lot.
[02:34] Mark Rivera: We plan to pin model to a 7B v2 for chat initially, with a heavier 13B for more nuanced responses later.
[02:41] Alex Monroe: Cool. Let's talk concurrency — 150-200 concurrents. Is that 150 steady concurrent token streams or 150 concurrent requests?
[02:50] Mark Rivera: Concurrent open streams — so they're holding a streaming socket while tokens arrive.
[02:55] Priya Kapoor: Important distinction. Open sockets hold compute state (KV cache) per connection; that affects memory and GPU capacity planning for Dedicated or Private. For Hosted we can do autoscaling but you pay for warm KV cache and memory footprint.
[03:10] Tom Li: What's the typical tokens/sec throughput we can expect from Redwood for batch jobs? Our nightly job is about 2 billion tokens and needs to finish in a 3-hour window.
[03:20] Samir Patel: On A100-class instances with optimized kernels and batching, you can see something like 1-2 million tokens/sec aggregate per GPU for smaller precisions/quantized models, but that number varies a lot by model, seq length, and batch efficiency. For your 2B tokens in 3 hours you need ~185 tokens/sec sustained aggregate? Sorry math slip — let me calc.
[03:36] Samir Patel: (quick math) 2,000,000,000 tokens / (3 * 3600 seconds) = ~185,000 tokens/sec. So you would need a cluster sized accordingly; e.g., a handful of GPUs with high batching efficiency.
[03:52] Elena Gomez: 185k tokens/sec sounds doable but depends on batch size. What about cost differences between Hosted and Dedicated?
[04:00] Alex Monroe: Hosted can be efficient because we multi-tenant and schedule batches across many requests, lowering cost per token; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and latency SLOs because capacity is reserved. For heavy batch workloads you might prefer Dedicated to control job scheduling windows and network egress.
[04:13] Mark Rivera: Also curious about Private — we have regulatory constraints and would need VPC + KMS and SOC2 proofs.
[04:21] Priya Kapoor: We support Private with a customer-controlled VPC and KMS/HSM integrations. From a perf standpoint Private can match Dedicated if you provision similar hardware; the difference is operational ownership. We can share SOC2, ISO docs and a network diagram after the call.
[04:36] Alex Monroe: Quick note — sometimes the p95 target is measured client-side and includes network. We recommend splitting targets: 1) model inference p95 and 2) end-to-end p95 including app latency.
[04:48] Nina Park: For stakeholders, the product team cares about end-to-end p95. Infra cares about model inference. We'll provide both when we share SLOs.
[05:02] Mark Rivera: On KV cache — we want prefix caching for repeated context between messages. How much does that reduce latency?
[05:09] Priya Kapoor: Prefix/KV caching can dramatically reduce per-token compute for repeated instruction/context; first token still needs the initial KV fill but subsequent tokens are cheap. For chat with small deltas, you can see 20-40% per-token latency reduction depending on cache hit rates.
[05:24] Tom Li: Does Redwood do automatic fallbacks when capacity is saturated? For instance downgrade to a quantized variant?
[05:30] Alex Monroe: Yes, our smart routing can fall back to compatible model variants based on policy (latency, cost, region). For critical flows we recommend a canary/fallback policy so you never drop sessions.
[05:42] Mark Rivera: Ok. Can we get baseline numbers — e.g., 7B quantized on Hosted p50/p95 for 32-token responses with streaming?
[05:50] Priya Kapoor: We'll run a tailored benchmark but as an example, a well-tuned 7B quantized model on our hosted infra often sees p50 ~60-80ms and p95 ~180-260ms for 32-token streaming responses, depending on network. Again, streaming first-byte may be much lower but full response tail is the p95.
[06:09] Elena Gomez: We might accept a 300ms customer-side p95 given mobile network variability, but it helps to keep inference under 200ms.
[06:16] Samir Patel: For concurrency sizing with open streams, you'll want to think about GPU memory per connection. We usually compute estimate: memory footprint per connection * concurrent = capacity needed plus headroom. We'll provide a worksheet.
[06:28] Mark Rivera: Great. On batching — how do you handle batching with streaming? We need low latency but batching increases throughput.
[06:36] Priya Kapoor: We use continuous batching and adaptive policies. For streaming short sequences we favor small micro-batches to hit low latency; for background batch jobs we use large effective batch sizes to max tokens/sec. You can configure batch windows and max latency tolerances in Dedicated.
[06:55] Tom Li: For our nightly job, can Redwood run it in Hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[07:01] Alex Monroe: Both are possible. Hosted is fine for many customers; however, if you need guaranteed completion within a specific window and predictable cost, Dedicated is typically recommended. We can also run mixed mode — Hosted for chat and Dedicated/Private for large batch jobs.
[07:15] Mark Rivera: Let's talk benchmarks. We'd like Redwood to run a short set: 1) 7B quantized streaming 32-token p50/p95 with 150 concurrent streams, 2) batch throughput for 2B tokens scaled to 3-hour window. Is that doable?
[07:29] Priya Kapoor: Yes we can. We'll need sample prompts, token distribution, and a representative client pattern. Also confirm whether you want the test on Hosted infra or simulated Dedicated hardware.
[07:40] Mark Rivera: Start with Hosted so we can see multi-tenant numbers, then run Dedicated simulation.
[07:45] Priya Kapoor: Perfect. We'll prepare a harness and share the scripts (JMeter/locust style) and a results dashboard.
[07:53] Elena Gomez: On security docs, we'll need the SOC2 certification, encryption at rest details, and KMS integration notes — especially for Private.
[07:59] Alex Monroe: We'll bundle those and Priya will share the network and KMS docs.
[08:04] Tom Li: Any gotchas with streaming and SSO or auth? We use mTLS and token-based auth.
[08:10] Samir Patel: We support mTLS and SSO — you'll set up SAML/SSO for the console and service tokens for the inference calls. For Private you'll host the control plane in your VPC. We'll share auth patterns in the doc pack.
[08:22] Mark Rivera: Cost sensitivity — are there knobs we should tune to balance cost vs latency? Quantization? Batching windows? Model variants?
[08:30] Priya Kapoor: All of the above. Quantization reduces memory and can reduce latency but can affect quality. Batching window increases throughput but hurts latency. Model variants let you route low-criticality traffic to cheaper models. Our Redwood Optimize tool can make recommendations based on your traffic.
[08:46] Nina Park: Who's the internal Redwood contact for getting the benchmark scheduled and the pricing quote?
[08:50] Alex Monroe: That's me for pricing and can loop in finance; Priya will run the benchmarks and provide the technical report. I'll follow up with a calendar invite for next week to review results and pricing.
[09:02] Mark Rivera: Sounds good. A couple of quick clarifying Qs from my team — how do you report latency metrics? Do you provide token-level traces?
[09:10] Priya Kapoor: We provide per-request latency breakdowns (queue, execution, kernel time, network). Token-level traces are available for streaming sessions in the debug logs if needed, and we can export to your tracing system.
[09:20] Elena Gomez: And billing for Dedicated — is it flat reserved capacity plus usage?
[09:25] Alex Monroe: Dedicated is typically a reserved monthly commit with overage and burst pricing options; we'll include illustrative numbers in the quote.
[09:33] Mark Rivera: Ok, that's all I have. Any final notes?
[09:36] Priya Kapoor: We'll include sample run configs: concurrency=150, stream window=20ms, batch window=50ms for low-latency tests, and a large-batch config for nightly jobs.
[09:48] Alex Monroe: I'll send the benchmark plan, Priya will send security docs, and Mark will send the traffic profile. We'll reconvene in one week. Thanks everyone.
[09:55] Tom Li: Thanks, appreciate it.
[10:00] Mark Rivera: Thanks.
[47:00] /* Call ended */
